comment: The missed distinction was B’s single, delayed normalization versus A/D’s heavier early normalization—not residual connectivity. B can retain more coordinate-scale information while developing interaction features; early LayerNorm may introduce distractor-dependent scaling. This is a plausible explanation, not an established causal result. K1018 helped correctly place GELU candidate C first and warned that more normalization is unreliable here; I nevertheless overfavored A/D. Backtesting found fewer-LN wins in 2/2 matched-depth corpus pairs, but activations were not controlled; matched lab comparisons were sparse. Crucially, a controlled 8-feature XOR experiment at Adam lr×steps=0.0512 contradicted the proposed rule: D-like 0.2196 < A-like 0.2210 < B-like 0.2244. No robust new rule is justified.

The missed comparison was C versus D: equal LayerNorm counts do not imply equal optimization benefits. C normalizes before its first hidden transformation, has greater width, and uses GELU; these plausibly enable faster nonlinear feature learning than D’s narrower SiLU network with normalization only in its middle block. I over-weighted D’s extra depth and residual connections. K1009 helped identify the low-update regime and A’s disadvantage; K1014 helped prioritize E’s additional normalization but actually cautioned against a depth preference on piecewise boundaries. Backtesting found only one qualifying shallow-GELU/deeper-SiLU corpus comparison (a win), none on piecewise boundaries, and no matched lab pairs. That is insufficient to establish a general C-over-D rule.

All choices share Δ=0.00768. I overcredited residual connections: C’s three LayerNorms and normalized final block beat A’s two-LN residual stack. K1006 helped; K1015’s blanket prohibition against deep plain classification stacks misled. Backtesting XOR at Δ<0.05, input dimension<8, and matched optimizer type/lr/budget: last-normalized plain stacks with at least as many LNs won 18/19 historical comparisons; lab comparisons matched on optimizer type/lr won 5/6 across six sets. The lab edge reversed above Δ=0.05 (1/5 wins). However, C beating B despite fewer LNs remains unexplained: analogous historical fewer-LN comparisons won 0/6. Thus the evidence supports correcting C versus A, not a general rule predicting the complete gold order.
